title: Raising children alone in Latin America and the Caribbean: strong mothers and weak social assistance
gist: A new World Bank study finds lone-mother households in Latin America and the Caribbean grew 46% over 15 years and face nearly double the regional poverty rate, driven less by low labor participation than by informal, low-quality jobs and threadbare public support (only 7% of household income).

insights.claim: In Latin America and the Caribbean, the share of households with children headed solely by the mother rose from about 7% to nearly 10% between 2007 and 2022, a 46% increase in a decade and a half, so close to one in ten children in the region now grows up in a lone-mother household.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A structural, accelerating shift in household composition raises demand for childcare, cash-transfer and labor-formalization policy across the region — relevant for social-spending and consumer-market planning.
insights.quote: Over the past fifteen years, the share of households with children where the mother is the only adult (i.e. lone mother households) has grown from 7% to nearly 10%.
insights.locator: Fact 1: Lone-mother households in Latin America and the Caribbean are on the rise.

insights.claim: Prevalence of lone-mother households varies widely by country, from 5.3% in Honduras to 14.1% in the Dominican Republic, meaning national policy responses cannot be one-size-fits-all across the region.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Country-level dispersion means social-protection reform priority and fiscal exposure differ sharply between LAC markets.
insights.locator: This regional average varies across countries, from 5.3% in Honduras to 14.1% in the Dominican Republic.

themes.theme: A Deep and Structural Poverty Gap

insights.claim: Lone-mother households in LAC face a 45.5% poverty rate versus a 26.8% regional average (measured against the US$8.30/person/day 2021-PPP line), and in Brazil, Colombia, Honduras and Peru more than half of lone-mother households are poor.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A near-double poverty rate concentrated in a fast-growing household type signals a widening, durable pocket of demand for targeted cash-transfer and childcare subsidy programs.
insights.locator: Fact 2: Poverty hits lone mothers and their children hard.

insights.claim: The authors argue the poverty gap is not simply because lone mothers earn less, but because they face a combination of disadvantages — job quality, childcare access, and thin transfers — that public policy has so far failed to address.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Frames the policy problem as multi-dimensional rather than purely an earnings gap, implying single-lever fixes (e.g. minimum wage alone) will underperform.
insights.quote: This is not simply because lone mothers earn less; it is because they face a combination of disadvantages that public policy has so far failed to adequately address.
insights.locator: Fact 2: Poverty hits lone mothers and their children hard.

insights.claim: Lone mothers derive nearly 60% of household income from their own labor earnings and about 40% from private transfers (non-resident fathers, relatives) plus public assistance — but public assistance contributes only 7% of income, versus roughly 80% of income coming from jobs in households where women raise children with another adult present.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Quantifies how thin the social safety net is for this group — a 7-point public-assistance share is a concrete benchmark for evaluating whether cash-transfer expansions are material.
insights.locator: On average, nearly 60% of household income comes from the lone mother's labor earnings.

insights.claim: Private transfers, which include child support payments from non-resident fathers, account for just 13% of total household income in lone-mother households, indicating financial support from absent fathers falls well short of what is needed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A quantified enforcement gap — 13% of income — gives a concrete target for child-support-enforcement policy reform to close.
insights.locator: Private transfers (which include child support payments) account for just 13% of total household income.

themes.theme: Working Hard, But in Low-Quality Jobs

insights.claim: More than four in five lone mothers in LAC participate in the labor force, versus about three in five women who share childrearing with another adult at home — so the poverty gap is not a labor-force-participation problem.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rules out a simple 'women aren't working' explanation, redirecting the policy and investment lens toward job quality and childcare access instead.
insights.locator: More than four in five lone mothers participate in the labor force, compared to about three in five women who count on other adults at home to raise children.

insights.claim: Lone mothers are 10% more likely than mothers who share childrearing with another adult to work in the informal economy, and more than one in four lone mothers are classified as 'working poor' — employed but still unable to make ends meet.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: High informality among an already-large and growing household segment signals a structural drag on formal-sector labor supply and payroll-tax bases in LAC.
insights.locator: More than one in four lone mothers are "working poor", meaning they have a job but still cannot make ends meet.

insights.claim: Without access to reliable childcare, lone mothers cannot take on formal jobs that require full-time hours, which the authors identify as the key mechanism trapping them in lower-paid informal work.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Identifies childcare — not skills or willingness to work — as the binding constraint, pointing directly at childcare-subsidy programs as the highest-leverage intervention.
insights.locator: Without access to quality childcare, lone mothers often cannot take on better-paying formal employment.

insights.claim: The authors' central policy recommendation is that childcare access is 'perhaps the single most powerful policy lever available' to raise lone mothers' incomes and financial security, though how to finance it remains an open question.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Signals where World Bank-aligned LAC governments are likely to direct social-spending reform — a leading indicator for childcare-sector public investment and PPP opportunities.
insights.quote: childcare access is perhaps the single most powerful policy lever available
insights.locator: 1. First, childcare access is perhaps the single most powerful policy lever available.

insights.claim: The authors call for expanding and better targeting conditional cash transfers toward lone mothers, since the current 7% public-assistance income share is judged insufficient to meaningfully reduce their poverty rate.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable policy ask — cash-transfer targeting reform — with a quantified baseline (7%) against which future reform can be benchmarked.
insights.locator: Expanding and improving the targeting of conditional cash could directly reduce poverty rates of these families.
